question: A 36-hour-old neonate delivered at a district hospital has an axillary temperature of 35.2°C. The nurse asks you to classify this finding. Which classification and immediate management priority is CORRECT?

answers.text: Normal — no action needed; axillary temperature is always 0.5°C lower than core temperature, so 35.2°C represents a core temperature of 35.7°C, which is within normal limits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 35.2°C axillary temperature IS hypothermia, regardless of the axillary-core differential. Normal axillary temperature in a neonate is 36.5–37.5°C. A temperature of 35.2°C falls in the moderate hypothermia range (32–36°C) and requires active warming. The axillary-core correction does not bring this into the normal range.

answers.text: Moderate hypothermia (32–36°C); initiate skin-to-skin Kangaroo Mother Care and check blood glucose immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Normal neonatal axillary temperature = 36.5–37.5°C. Mild hypothermia = 36–36.4°C; moderate hypothermia = 32–36°C; severe hypothermia = <32°C. At 35.2°C this is moderate hypothermia. Skin-to-skin KMC is the safest and most effective rewarming method. Blood glucose MUST be checked immediately — hypothermia and hypoglycaemia frequently co-exist and compound each other.

answers.text: Mild hypothermia (36–36.4°C); add an extra layer of clothing and reassess in 2 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 35.2°C falls below the mild hypothermia threshold (36–36.4°C) — this is moderate hypothermia. A temperature of 35.2°C requires active warming (KMC/radiant warmer) and urgent blood glucose check, not just an extra layer with a 2-hour delay.

answers.text: Severe hypothermia (<32°C); intubate and begin active external rewarming with a warming blanket at 40°C

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 35.2°C is above the severe hypothermia threshold of <32°C. Rapid active external warming (e.g. 40°C blanket) carries a risk of rewarming hypotension. For moderate hypothermia, gradual rewarming via KMC or a radiant warmer at a set point that is 1°C above the infant's current temperature is preferred. Intubation is not indicated solely for moderate hypothermia.

overallFeedback.feedback: Normal neonatal axillary temperature: 36.5–37.5°C. Moderate hypothermia: 32–36°C (includes 35.2°C). Immediate management: KMC skin-to-skin + urgent blood glucose check. Severe hypothermia is <32°C and needs more intensive rewarming.

Correct. 35.2°C = moderate hypothermia (32–36°C). Immediate actions: skin-to-skin KMC, check blood glucose (hypoglycaemia co-exists frequently), and monitor temperature every 30 minutes until ≥36.5°C.
